title: Anypoint Platform Components
description: Go beyond building flows and explore the full Anypoint Platform: Runtime Manager, environments, access management, Exchange, Design Center, monitoring, CLI and secrets management.

subtopics.title: Runtime Manager Overview
subtopics.meta_description: Learn how Anypoint Runtime Manager gives you a single console to deploy, manage, and monitor Mule applications across CloudHub, Runtime Fabric, and standalone runtimes.
subtopics.summary: Runtime Manager is the operational control plane of Anypoint Platform, letting you deploy, scale, and observe Mule applications no matter which type of runtime they live on.
subtopics.content_html:
Once a Mule application is built, someone has to deploy it, keep it running, and know the moment it stops behaving. That someone is usually not touching Anypoint Studio at all — they are looking at Runtime Manager, the console inside Anypoint Platform that manages the full lifecycle of deployed applications regardless of where those applications physically run.

One Console, Three Target Types

Runtime Manager's defining feature is that it abstracts away the target runtime. Whether an application is deployed to CloudHub (MuleSoft's managed iPaaS), Runtime Fabric (a containerized runtime plane you operate on your own Kubernetes cluster or VMs), or a standalone/hybrid Mule runtime installed on a server you administer directly, it shows up in the same Applications list with the same basic actions: start, stop, restart, undeploy, view logs, and view properties.

TargetWho manages infrastructureTypical use case
CloudHubMuleSoftFast time-to-market, standard cloud workloads
Runtime FabricYou (cluster/VMs), MuleSoft (container platform)Data residency with cloud-like elasticity
Standalone / HybridYouLegacy data centers, strict compliance, air-gapped networks

The Applications List

The Applications view is the first screen most operations engineers land on. For each deployed application it surfaces the environment it belongs to, its current status (Started, Failed, Deploying, Undeployed), the Mule runtime version, the worker size or replica count, and the last deployment timestamp. From here you can trigger a redeploy with a new artifact, roll back to a previous version, or adjust replicas/vCores without touching the underlying infrastructure directly.

Logs and Diagnostics

Runtime Manager aggregates application logs centrally so you do not have to SSH into a worker or a Kubernetes pod. You can search log output, filter by severity, download log files for offline analysis, and, on CloudHub, correlate logs with worker restarts. For deeper diagnostics, Runtime Manager also exposes thread dumps and, on some deployment models, JVM metrics that help pinpoint memory leaks or stuck threads before they cause an outage.

Alerts

Alerts let you get notified proactively instead of discovering a problem from an angry business user. You can configure alerts for conditions such as an application being undeployed unexpectedly, high memory usage, a worker restart, or certificate expiration approaching, and route notifications to email or, via webhook-based integrations, to tools like Slack or PagerDuty.

Tip: Configure an alert for certificate expiration on any application terminating TLS. Expired certificates are one of the most common, and most avoidable, causes of unplanned downtime.

Deploying From Runtime Manager

You can deploy a new application directly from Runtime Manager by uploading a packaged Mule application (a JAR built by Maven) or by selecting an asset already published to Exchange. Deployment properties — environment variables, JVM arguments, and application properties — are set per environment here, which is what allows the same artifact to be promoted from Sandbox to Production without rebuilding it.


# Example: deploying with the Mule Maven plugin, which ultimately talks to Runtime Manager's API
mvn deploy \
  -DmuleDeploy \
  -Danypoint.username=$ANYPOINT_USER \
  -Danypoint.password=$ANYPOINT_PASS \
  -Denvironment=Sandbox \
  -Dcloudhub.workers=2 \
  -Dcloudhub.workerType=micro

Why It Matters

Without Runtime Manager, an organization running a mix of cloud and on-premise Mule applications would need separate tooling per environment. Runtime Manager unifies that operational surface, which is precisely why it is the tool integration architects reach for when someone asks, "is this API up, and what version is running in Production right now?"

Key Points

  • Runtime Manager is Anypoint Platform's single console for deploying, managing, and monitoring Mule applications.
  • It works uniformly across CloudHub, Runtime Fabric, and standalone/hybrid runtimes.
  • The Applications list shows status, version, and sizing, and supports redeploy/rollback actions.
  • Centralized logs and thread dumps speed up troubleshooting without direct server access.
  • Alerts notify teams of undeploys, resource pressure, and certificate expiration before they become incidents.

subtopics.title: Environments and Business Groups
subtopics.meta_description: Understand how Anypoint Platform environments (Sandbox, Production, and custom environments) and Business Groups organize access, ownership, and deployments.
subtopics.summary: Environments isolate deployments and API instances by stage, while Business Groups isolate ownership and access across teams and sub-organizations.
subtopics.content_html:
Anypoint Platform organizations rarely stay simple for long. As soon as more than one team ships integrations, or an application needs to move safely from a developer's test run to a live production workload, two organizing concepts start doing the heavy lifting: environments and Business Groups.

Environments: Isolating by Stage

An environment is a logical partition within an Anypoint Platform organization (or sub-organization) used to isolate deployed applications, API instances, and their configuration from one another. Every organization starts with two default environments, Sandbox and Production, but you are free to create additional custom environments — QA, UAT, Staging, Performance — to match your actual release pipeline.

Deployments, API Manager API instances, Object Stores, and VPC assignments are all scoped to a specific environment. This means the same packaged Mule application can be deployed independently into Sandbox and Production, each with its own connection credentials, scaling settings, and policies, without any risk of a test call accidentally hitting a production backend.

Environment typePurposeTypical characteristics
SandboxDevelopment and integration testingSmaller worker sizes, test credentials, relaxed policies
Custom (QA/UAT)Pre-production validationMirrors production topology at smaller scale
ProductionLive trafficRestricted deployment access, full monitoring and alerting

Promoting Across Environments

Because environments are just deployment targets, promoting an application from Sandbox to Production typically means redeploying the same immutable artifact with different environment-specific properties, rather than rebuilding it. This is what makes environment-scoped properties (set in Runtime Manager or injected via a CI/CD pipeline) so important — they are the mechanism that keeps one build artifact usable everywhere.

Business Groups: Isolating by Ownership

Where environments separate applications by deployment stage, Business Groups (also called sub-organizations) separate the platform by team, business unit, or line of business. A Business Group is a nested organization inside the root Anypoint Platform organization with its own environments, its own set of users and roles, and its own asset ownership in Exchange.

A large enterprise might structure Business Groups by department — Finance, HR, Supply Chain — so that each team manages its own APIs and applications, sets its own access rules, and only shares assets deliberately by publishing them to Exchange with the right visibility settings. The root organization's administrators retain oversight (they can see usage and billing across all sub-orgs) without every team needing full administrative rights to every other team's environments.

How the Two Interact

Business Groups and environments compose: each Business Group has its own set of environments, and permissions can be scoped to a specific combination of Business Group and environment. A developer might have Deploy rights in the Payments Business Group's Sandbox environment, but only read access to its Production environment, while having no access at all to the Marketing Business Group.

Note: Assets published to Exchange are owned by the Business Group (organization ID) that published them, which is why asset group IDs in Exchange often map directly to a team's Business Group.

Why It Matters

Getting this structure right early prevents two common failure modes: teams accidentally interfering with each other's production traffic, and an organization that is so locked down that nobody can self-serve deployments. Environments and Business Groups together give you the isolation boundaries to avoid both.

Key Points

  • Environments (Sandbox, Production, and custom ones) isolate deployments and API instances by release stage.
  • The same build artifact is typically promoted across environments with different environment-scoped properties.
  • Business Groups isolate ownership, users, and asset publishing rights across teams or sub-organizations.
  • Permissions can be scoped to a specific Business Group and environment combination.
  • Exchange asset ownership is tied to the Business Group that published the asset.

subtopics.title: VPC and Networking in Anypoint Platform
subtopics.meta_description: Learn how CloudHub Virtual Private Cloud, static IPs, VPC peering, and dedicated load balancers let Mule applications securely reach on-premise and cloud systems.
subtopics.summary: CloudHub networking features, from VPC and static IPs to dedicated load balancers, control exactly how Mule applications are reached and what they can reach in return.
subtopics.content_html:
A Mule application deployed to CloudHub does not live in isolation — it usually needs to call a database behind a corporate firewall, be reachable only from a partner's whitelisted IP range, or terminate TLS under the company's own domain name. Anypoint Platform's networking features exist to make those requirements possible without giving up the operational simplicity of a managed iPaaS.

Virtual Private Cloud (VPC)

A CloudHub Virtual Private Cloud is a logically isolated network segment, provisioned with its own CIDR block, into which your organization's CloudHub workers are deployed. Instead of sitting on CloudHub's shared network, applications in a VPC get private IP addresses and can be placed behind firewall rules you control. A VPC is the prerequisite for almost every other advanced networking feature CloudHub offers.

Static IP Addresses

By default, CloudHub workers can be assigned dynamic outbound IPs that change on redeploy, which is a problem when a downstream partner or backend system whitelists specific IP addresses. Within a VPC, you can reserve static IP addresses for outbound traffic, so that firewall rules on the receiving system never need to be updated when you redeploy or rescale.

VPC Peering and On-Premise Connectivity

A CloudHub VPC can be peered with a VPC in your own AWS account, or connected back to an on-premise data center through a VPN tunnel or a dedicated private-circuit connection analogous to AWS Direct Connect. This is what allows a Mule application running on CloudHub to call an on-premise Oracle database or a legacy SOAP service as if it were on the same network, without ever exposing that backend system to the public internet.

PatternUse case
VPC peeringConnect CloudHub to another VPC in your own AWS account
Site-to-site VPNConnect CloudHub to an on-premise data center over an encrypted tunnel
Dedicated private connectionHigh-throughput, low-latency link that bypasses the public internet entirely

Whitelisting and Firewall Rules

Within a VPC you define inbound and outbound firewall rules controlling which IP ranges and ports can reach your workers, and which destinations your workers are permitted to call. This lets you enforce, for example, that an application exposing a partner-facing API only accepts inbound traffic from a specific set of partner IP addresses.

Dedicated Load Balancers

The shared CloudHub load balancer is included at no extra cost but only supports CloudHub's own generated domain names and shared wildcard TLS certificates. A Dedicated Load Balancer (DLB) is an add-on that gives you a custom domain name, your own TLS certificate, path-based routing across multiple applications, and control over TLS versions and cipher suites — all commonly required for a production-facing customer or partner API.


# Conceptual example of DLB-related settings tracked alongside a CloudHub deployment
deployment:
  vpc: prod-vpc-usw2
  staticIp: true
  dedicatedLoadBalancer:
    domain: api.example.com
    tlsContext: exchange-managed-tls-context
    mappings:
      - path: /orders/*
        app: orders-api
      - path: /payments/*
        app: payments-api

Why It Matters

Networking is frequently the difference between a proof of concept and a production-ready deployment. A design that ignores VPC placement, static IPs, and load balancer strategy tends to surface as a networking emergency during go-live, not during development.

Tip: Decide on VPC and load balancer strategy before development starts, not after — retrofitting static IPs or a dedicated domain onto an already-deployed application usually requires a redeploy and DNS cutover window.

Key Points

  • A CloudHub VPC isolates workers onto a private network segment you control.
  • Static IP addresses give downstream systems a stable address to whitelist.
  • VPC peering and VPN/private-connection patterns let CloudHub reach on-premise systems securely.
  • Firewall rules restrict both inbound access to and outbound access from your workers.
  • Dedicated load balancers add custom domains, your own TLS certificates, and path-based routing.

subtopics.title: Access Management and Roles (RBAC)
subtopics.meta_description: See how Anypoint Access Management uses users, teams, roles, and permissions to control who can deploy applications, manage APIs, or administer the organization.
subtopics.summary: Access Management applies role-based access control across Anypoint Platform, governing exactly who can deploy, view, or administer resources in each environment.
subtopics.content_html:
Every capability covered elsewhere in this category — deploying an application, publishing to Exchange, editing an API policy — is gated by a permission somewhere. Access Management is the part of Anypoint Platform where those permissions are actually configured, through a fairly conventional but important role-based access control (RBAC) model.

Users and Teams

Individual users can be added directly to an Anypoint Platform organization, or, more commonly in larger organizations, grouped into Teams so that permissions can be assigned once to the team rather than repeatedly to each person. Teams are especially useful when combined with Business Groups: a "Payments Integration Team" can be granted deployment rights to the Payments Business Group's Sandbox environment as a single assignment.

Roles and Permissions

A role is a named bundle of permissions that can be assigned to a user or a team, scoped to an organization, a Business Group, or a specific environment. Anypoint Platform ships with a set of built-in roles covering the most common needs:

Built-in roleWhat it typically grants
Organization AdministratorFull control over the org, including billing, users, and all Business Groups
Environment Manager / AdminManage applications and settings within an assigned environment
API Manager / API Version OwnerManage API instances, apply and edit policies in API Manager
Exchange Contributor / ViewerPublish and edit, or only view, assets in Exchange
Design Center DeveloperCreate and edit API specifications and Flow Designer projects

When built-in roles do not line up exactly with how your organization is structured, Access Management lets administrators define custom roles that combine a specific set of permissions — for example, a role that can view Production applications and logs but cannot deploy or undeploy anything.

What RBAC Actually Controls

In practice, roles determine things like whether a given user can:

  • Deploy or undeploy an application in a specific environment.
  • View, but not modify, application logs and metrics.
  • Create, edit, or apply policies to an API instance in API Manager.
  • Publish new versions of an asset to Exchange.
  • Invite or remove users, and assign roles to others (an administrative permission itself).

Single Sign-On and Federation

Rather than managing passwords directly, most enterprise Anypoint Platform organizations federate authentication to an external identity provider using SAML 2.0 or OpenID Connect — commonly Okta, Azure AD, or Ping Identity. Users authenticate against the corporate identity provider, and Anypoint Platform maps the resulting identity to platform roles, often driven by group membership passed in the SAML assertion or OIDC claims. This keeps user provisioning and de-provisioning centralized in the identity provider rather than duplicated inside Anypoint Platform.

Note: Federated SSO handles authentication (who you are); Access Management's roles still handle authorization (what you can do), so both need to be configured correctly for federation to be useful.

Why It Matters

Getting RBAC wrong in either direction is costly: too permissive, and a junior developer can accidentally undeploy a production API; too restrictive, and every deployment becomes a ticket to a platform team. Deliberate role design, especially combined with environment and Business Group scoping, is what lets organizations scale self-service without losing control.

Key Points

  • Access Management governs users, teams, roles, and permissions across Anypoint Platform.
  • Roles can be scoped to an organization, a Business Group, or a specific environment.
  • Built-in roles cover common needs; custom roles fill in the gaps for specific responsibilities.
  • RBAC controls deployment rights, API policy management, Exchange publishing, and administrative actions.
  • SSO/federation (SAML, OIDC) typically handles authentication while Access Management still handles authorization.

subtopics.title: Anypoint Exchange: Publishing and Reusing Assets
subtopics.meta_description: Explore Anypoint Exchange as the catalog for APIs, connectors, templates, and examples, and learn how teams publish, version, and discover reusable assets.
subtopics.summary: Anypoint Exchange is the searchable, governed catalog where teams publish and discover reusable APIs, connectors, templates, and fragments across the organization.
subtopics.content_html:
Reuse is one of the central promises of API-led connectivity, but reuse does not happen automatically just because two teams both use Mule. Someone has to publish an asset somewhere discoverable, describe what it does, and version it responsibly so consumers are not broken by silent changes. That somewhere is Anypoint Exchange.

What Lives in Exchange

Exchange is a searchable catalog of reusable assets across an organization. The asset types it hosts include:

  • REST APIs (RAML or OAS specifications), SOAP APIs (WSDL), and AsyncAPI specifications.
  • Connectors, both MuleSoft-built and custom connectors your organization has authored.
  • Templates and examples — runnable reference implementations for common integration patterns.
  • Fragments — reusable RAML/OAS pieces such as shared data types, traits, or security schemes.
  • Custom policies built for API Manager.

Every asset gets a detail page with documentation, an icon, tags, and, for API specifications, an interactive console for trying out endpoints directly from the browser.

Publishing an Asset

There are two common ways to publish. From Design Center, publishing an API specification to Exchange is a single click once the spec is in a working state. For assets built outside Design Center — a connector, a template, or a Mule application packaged as a reusable asset — publishing is done with the Exchange Maven plugin, typically as part of a CI/CD pipeline.


mvn deploy \
  -DskipTests \
  -DaltDeploymentRepository=exchange::default::https://maven.anypoint.mulesoft.com/api/v1/organizations/<org-id>/maven

The asset's groupId, artifactId, and version in its Maven coordinates map directly to how it is identified and versioned inside Exchange, which is also why the groupId is tied to the publishing Business Group's organization ID.

Versioning

Exchange follows semantic versioning conventions for most asset types. Publishing a new version does not remove old versions — consumers who depend on 1.2.0 keep working even after 1.3.0 is published, and Exchange shows a full version history so consumers can evaluate what changed before upgrading. This is what makes it safe for a shared connector or API fragment to evolve over time without breaking every downstream project simultaneously.

Discovering and Reusing Assets

Exchange's search and tagging make it possible for a developer starting a new project to check whether an equivalent integration already exists before building one from scratch. A discovered API specification can be pulled directly into Design Center to build a new implementation against; a discovered connector can be added straight into a Studio project's dependencies via its Maven coordinates; a discovered fragment can be referenced from a new RAML spec instead of redefining the same data type again.

Asset typeTypical consumer action
API specificationView docs, try console, generate a client, or implement against it
ConnectorAdd as a Maven dependency in a Mule project
TemplateClone into Studio as a starting point for a new project
FragmentReference from another RAML/OAS specification

Governance and Visibility

Asset visibility can be scoped to the publishing Business Group only, to the entire organization, or made public, depending on who should be able to find and use it. Exchange also integrates with API Manager so that an API specification published to Exchange can be registered as a governed API instance without re-entering its contract by hand.

Tip: Treat Exchange asset descriptions and examples as a product, not an afterthought — a well-documented asset gets reused; a poorly documented one gets rebuilt from scratch by the next team that needs it.

Why It Matters

Exchange is what turns individually well-built APIs and connectors into an organizational asset base. Without a shared, governed catalog, reuse depends entirely on informal knowledge of who built what, which does not scale past a handful of teams.

Key Points

  • Exchange is the searchable catalog for APIs, connectors, templates, examples, and fragments.
  • Assets are published from Design Center or via the Exchange Maven plugin as groupId/artifactId/version coordinates.
  • Semantic versioning lets an asset evolve without breaking existing consumers on older versions.
  • Search and tagging support discovery so teams reuse assets instead of rebuilding them.
  • Visibility scoping and API Manager integration add governance around what gets shared and how.

subtopics.title: Design Center Overview
subtopics.meta_description: Learn how Anypoint Design Center's API Designer and Flow Designer support design-first API development and low-code integration building.
subtopics.summary: Design Center houses API Designer for contract-first API specifications and Flow Designer for building integrations in the browser, both feeding directly into Exchange.
subtopics.content_html:
Not every integration decision should require opening a full IDE. Design Center is Anypoint Platform's browser-based workspace for two related but distinct activities: designing API contracts before implementation, and building simpler integration flows without leaving the browser at all.

API Designer

API Designer is the tool most teams reach for first inside Design Center. It provides a split-pane editor for writing a RAML or OAS (OpenAPI) specification, with a live-rendered documentation preview next to the raw code, plus autocomplete, inline validation, and example/mock generation. Because it is a genuine code editor underneath the visual layer, experienced API designers can drop into raw RAML/OAS at any point rather than being limited to a purely graphical builder.


#%RAML 1.0
title: Orders API
version: v1
baseUri: https://api.example.com/orders/{version}
types:
  Order:
    properties:
      id: string
      status: string
      total: number
/orders:
  get:
    responses:
      200:
        body:
          application/json:
            type: Order[]

API Designer also supports mocking: as soon as a spec has example responses defined, Design Center exposes a mocking service URL, which lets frontend or consumer teams start integrating against the contract before a single line of the actual implementation exists.

Design-First API Lifecycle

API Designer is the entry point of MuleSoft's design-first approach to API-led connectivity: define the contract, get feedback from consumers against the mock, iterate on the RAML/OAS, and only then implement it — either by hand-coding a Mule application against the spec using APIkit, or generating scaffolding directly from it. This ordering avoids the common failure mode where an API's shape is dictated entirely by whatever the implementation happened to produce first.

Flow Designer

Flow Designer is Design Center's low-code canvas for building actual integration logic — connecting a trigger (like an HTTP listener or a scheduled poll) to a sequence of steps such as transforming data, calling a connector, or branching on a condition, all through a drag-and-drop interface in the browser. It is aimed at simpler integrations and citizen-integrator scenarios where spinning up Anypoint Studio is more overhead than the task warrants, though it deploys the resulting application to CloudHub just like a Studio-built project.

How the Two Fit Together

ToolPrimary outputTypical user
API DesignerRAML/OAS specificationAPI designers, architects
Flow DesignerDeployable Mule application (low-code)Citizen integrators, smaller integrations
Anypoint StudioDeployable Mule application (full IDE)Mule developers building complex flows

Publishing to Exchange

Both API Designer and Flow Designer projects can be published to Exchange directly from Design Center. Publishing an API specification makes it discoverable and consumable by other teams immediately, and it can be registered as a managed API instance in API Manager without leaving the platform's web interface.

Note: An API specification published from Design Center is not automatically an enforced, running API — it still needs to be registered as an instance in API Manager and have an implementation deployed behind it.

Why It Matters

Design Center lowers the barrier to starting an integration project correctly: an API contract reviewed and mocked before implementation, or a straightforward integration built without provisioning a full development environment. Both paths funnel into the same governed platform rather than existing as disconnected side tools.

Key Points

  • Design Center bundles API Designer (contract-first RAML/OAS editing) and Flow Designer (low-code integrations).
  • API Designer supports live docs, validation, and mocking to support a design-first workflow.
  • Flow Designer builds and deploys simpler CloudHub integrations directly from the browser.
  • Both tools publish their output to Exchange for discovery and reuse.
  • A published API specification still needs an API Manager instance and a running implementation to be a live API.

subtopics.title: Anypoint Monitoring and API Monitoring
subtopics.meta_description: See how Anypoint Monitoring's dashboards and alerts, together with API Manager's API Analytics, provide visibility into application health and API traffic.
subtopics.summary: Anypoint Monitoring tracks application-level health and performance, while API Analytics in API Manager tracks API-level traffic, consumers, and policy behavior.
subtopics.content_html:
Deploying an application is only the beginning; knowing how it is actually behaving in production is a separate, ongoing job. Anypoint Platform splits that job into two complementary lenses: Anypoint Monitoring, which looks at application and infrastructure health, and API Analytics inside API Manager, which looks at API traffic and consumer behavior.

Anypoint Monitoring: Application Health

Anypoint Monitoring provides built-in dashboards for every deployed application showing metrics like throughput (requests per minute), average and percentile response times, error rates, memory usage, and CPU utilization, without requiring any extra instrumentation code in the Mule application itself. These dashboards pull from the same runtime data Runtime Manager surfaces, but present it with more history and more granular time windows for trend analysis.

Custom Dashboards

Beyond the default views, Anypoint Monitoring lets you build custom dashboards that combine metrics across multiple applications — useful when a single business capability, like order processing, is implemented across several APIs at different layers of an API-led architecture (System, Process, Experience). A custom dashboard can put an Experience API's response time next to the System API it ultimately depends on, making it much faster to isolate where latency is actually introduced.

Alerts

Alert rules can be defined on the same metrics — for example, notify the on-call team if average response time exceeds 2 seconds for five consecutive minutes, or if error rate crosses 5%. Alerts are typically routed to email or forwarded to an incident management tool through a webhook, closing the loop between detection and response.

MetricWhat it signals
Response time (p95/p99)Tail latency affecting the slowest requests, often the first sign of trouble
Error rateApplication or downstream-dependency failures
Memory usageRisk of an OutOfMemoryError or a worker restart
ThroughputTraffic volume, useful for capacity planning

API Analytics: API-Level Visibility

Where Anypoint Monitoring looks at an application's internal health, API Analytics in API Manager looks at the API contract from the outside: which consumers (identified by client ID) are calling it, how often, which policies are being triggered (such as rate-limiting or spike control rejecting a request), and which response status codes are being returned. This is the data you would use to answer questions like "which client is closest to their rate limit" or "did this consumer stop calling our API after last month's deprecation notice."

API Analytics also supports building custom charts filtered by API version, resource path, or client application, which matters once an API has multiple active versions or partner-specific policy tiers running simultaneously.

How the Two Complement Each Other

A response-time spike visible in Anypoint Monitoring for an application tells you something is wrong; API Analytics can tell you whether that spike correlates with a specific consumer sending unusually large payloads, or with a particular endpoint being hit far more heavily than expected. Used together, they move troubleshooting from "the API is slow" to a specific, actionable cause.

Tip: Set alert thresholds based on your API's actual SLA, not arbitrary round numbers — an alert that fires constantly gets ignored, and one that never fires is useless.

Why It Matters

Production visibility is what turns "we shipped it" into "we know it is healthy." Combining application-level monitoring with API-level analytics gives both operations teams and API product owners the data they each actually need.

Key Points

  • Anypoint Monitoring provides built-in and custom dashboards for application throughput, latency, errors, and resource usage.
  • Alert rules on these metrics notify teams before minor issues become outages.
  • API Analytics in API Manager tracks API traffic, consumer behavior, and policy violations at the contract level.
  • Custom charts in API Analytics can be filtered by version, resource, or consuming application.
  • Application-level and API-level visibility together enable faster, more specific root-cause analysis.

subtopics.title: Anypoint CLI and Automation
subtopics.meta_description: Learn how anypoint-cli-v4 lets you script deployments, policy application, and Exchange operations, and how it fits into CI/CD pipelines alongside the Maven plugin.
subtopics.summary: Anypoint CLI puts Runtime Manager, API Manager, Exchange, and account operations behind scriptable commands, making it a natural fit for CI/CD automation.
subtopics.content_html:
Clicking through Runtime Manager works fine for a one-off deployment, but it does not scale to dozens of services deploying multiple times a day. That is the gap Anypoint CLI (anypoint-cli-v4) fills: a command-line interface that exposes most of what the Anypoint Platform web console can do as scriptable commands.

Installing and Authenticating

Anypoint CLI is distributed as an npm package and runs anywhere Node.js is available, which makes it easy to drop into virtually any CI/CD runner.


npm install -g anypoint-cli-v4

# Authenticate (interactive) or use a connected app / bearer token in CI
anypoint-cli-v4 account:login

In automated pipelines, interactive login is replaced with credentials supplied via a Connected App (client ID/secret) or an environment-provided bearer token, avoiding the need to store a personal username and password in pipeline secrets.

Command Surface

Commands are grouped by the Anypoint Platform capability they map to:

Command groupWhat it covers
runtime-mgrDeploy, undeploy, start/stop applications, list applications, view deployment status
api-mgrManage API instances, apply and configure policies, promote API versions
exchangeSearch, describe, and download assets from Anypoint Exchange
accountManage users, environments, and Business Group information

Scripting Common Operations

A typical use is redeploying an application as part of a release script, or applying a rate-limiting policy consistently across every environment an API is promoted through, instead of clicking through API Manager by hand each time.


# Deploy a packaged application to CloudHub
anypoint-cli-v4 runtime-mgr:cloudhub-application:deploy orders-api \
  --file target/orders-api-1.4.0.jar \
  --environment Sandbox \
  --runtime 4.4.0 \
  --workers 1 \
  --workerSize 0.2

# Apply a rate-limiting policy to an API instance
anypoint-cli-v4 api-mgr:policy:apply <api-instance-id> rate-limiting \
  --environment Production \
  --config '{"rateLimits":[{"maximumRequests":1000,"timePeriodInMilliseconds":60000}]}'

CLI vs the Maven Plugin

The Mule Maven plugin and Anypoint CLI overlap in that both can deploy applications, but they serve slightly different roles. The Maven plugin is invoked as part of a Maven build (mvn deploy) and is the natural fit when deployment is just one more phase of building the artifact itself. Anypoint CLI is standalone and better suited to operations that are not tied to a build — applying a policy, querying deployment status, searching Exchange, or orchestrating a multi-step release script that touches several unrelated commands.

CI/CD Integration

In practice, most pipelines use both: the Maven plugin builds and deploys the artifact as part of the build stage, while Anypoint CLI (or direct Platform APIs) handles surrounding automation such as promoting an API version, validating that a deployment succeeded before proceeding to the next stage, or tearing down a temporary Sandbox deployment after a pull-request build finishes.

Tip: Wrap CLI calls in pipeline scripts with explicit exit-code checks — a failed deploy that the pipeline does not notice will happily report a green build for a broken release.

Why It Matters

Automation through Anypoint CLI is what makes consistent, repeatable, auditable releases possible at scale. Manual console operations do not compose well into a pipeline; scripted CLI commands do.

Key Points

  • Anypoint CLI (anypoint-cli-v4) exposes Runtime Manager, API Manager, Exchange, and account operations as scriptable commands.
  • CI/CD pipelines authenticate with Connected Apps or tokens rather than interactive login.
  • It is commonly used to script deployments, apply policies consistently, and query deployment status.
  • The Maven plugin and Anypoint CLI are complementary, not redundant, in most pipelines.
  • Explicit success/failure checks around CLI calls keep pipelines from masking failed deployments.

subtopics.title: Secrets Manager
subtopics.meta_description: Understand how Anypoint Secrets Manager centrally manages TLS contexts, keystores, truststores, VPN configs, and secrets for CloudHub and Runtime Fabric applications.
subtopics.summary: Secrets Manager centralizes TLS contexts, keystores, truststores, and VPN configuration so sensitive material never has to be embedded directly in application properties.
subtopics.content_html:
Embedding a keystore password or a private key directly in an application's properties file is a well-known anti-pattern, but for a long time it was also the path of least resistance on CloudHub. Anypoint Secrets Manager exists to close that gap by giving TLS material and other sensitive configuration a proper, centrally managed home.

What Secrets Manager Manages

Secrets Manager centralizes several categories of sensitive configuration that Mule applications need at runtime but should not carry around as plain files or inline properties:

  • TLS contexts — the combination of a keystore (for presenting a certificate) and a truststore (for validating certificates presented by others), used by both inbound HTTPS listeners and outbound HTTPS requesters.
  • Keystores and truststores uploaded independently, referenced by multiple TLS contexts.
  • VPN device configurations, used when configuring the on-premise side of a VPC-connected VPN tunnel.
  • Unified secrets — generic key/value secrets (API keys, database credentials, tokens) that would otherwise sit in an application's deployment properties in plain text.

How Applications Use It

Rather than shipping a keystore file inside the deployable artifact, a CloudHub or Runtime Fabric application references a TLS context by name, and Secrets Manager supplies the actual certificate material at deploy time. This has two direct benefits: the certificate can be rotated centrally without rebuilding or redeploying every application that uses it, and the private key material is never checked into source control or visible in a build artifact.


<!-- Referencing a Secrets Manager-provisioned TLS context from an HTTP listener config -->
<http:listener-config name="https-listener-config">
  <http:listener-connection host="0.0.0.0" port="8081" protocol="HTTPS">
    <tls:context>
      <tls:key-store type="jks" alias="orders-api"
        keyPassword="${secure::secretsmanager.orders-api-keystore.password}" />
    </tls:context>
  </http:listener-connection>
</http:listener-config>

Centralized Rotation

Certificate expiration is one of the most common self-inflicted causes of production outages, and rotating a certificate that is copy-pasted across a dozen application property files is exactly the kind of manual process that gets missed. With Secrets Manager, rotating the underlying certificate in one place propagates to every application referencing that TLS context on their next restart or redeploy, without editing each application's configuration individually.

Without Secrets ManagerWith Secrets Manager
Keystore files bundled per applicationKeystores/truststores managed centrally, referenced by name
Certificate rotation means redeploying every applicationRotation happens once, applications pick it up automatically
Secrets risk exposure in build artifacts or logsSecrets never leave Secrets Manager in plaintext form

VPN Configuration Management

For organizations connecting a CloudHub VPC to an on-premise network, Secrets Manager also stores the VPN device configuration details (pre-shared keys, tunnel settings) needed to establish and maintain that connection, keeping that sensitive configuration out of general-purpose documentation or shared drives.

Access Control

Access to Secrets Manager entries is itself governed by Access Management roles, so that only authorized users or teams can view or rotate a given TLS context or secret, separate from who is permitted to deploy the applications that consume it.

Note: Secrets Manager stores and serves the secret material; it does not replace the need for good key hygiene upstream, such as generating strong keys and limiting who can request new certificates in the first place.

Why It Matters

As the number of deployed applications grows, manually tracked certificates and inline secrets become both a security risk and an operational burden. Secrets Manager turns that into a single governed source of truth that scales with the platform instead of against it.

Key Points

  • Secrets Manager centrally manages TLS contexts, keystores, truststores, VPN configs, and general secrets.
  • Applications reference secrets by name instead of embedding them in properties files or build artifacts.
  • Certificate rotation happens in one place and propagates to every referencing application.
  • It supports both CloudHub and Runtime Fabric deployment targets.
  • Access to secrets is itself governed by Access Management roles, independent of deployment permissions.
